claims.text: Interviewer-reported dyadic exposure: the interviewer discloses whether community or political-party representatives approached the interviewer (not the respondent) in connection with this fieldwork visit, so the observation is an interviewer's encounter with external mobilizers, not the respondent's own political contact.

evidence.quote: Were you approached by community and/or political party representatives?

claims.text: Affective threat is reported by the interviewer about the interviewer's own feeling during the interview; it records a felt state at interviewer grain, not an observed act or the respondent's fear.

evidence.quote: Did you feel threatened during the interview?

claims.text: Physically threatened is a distinct interviewer-side claim of bodily threat; it is separable from felt threat and from mere disruption, so a 'No' here does not negate a 'Yes' on felt threat.

evidence.quote: Were you physically threatened during the interview?

claims.text: Interviewer's retrospective characterization of the respondent's candor; the middle option is an explicit uncommitted judgment, not a mild version of adversarial candor, and refusal/don't-know are absent by design.

Forced-choice presidential legality item: respondents place themselves between presidential non-bindingness and presidential submission to laws and courts; the statement is conditional on the president's own belief, so the item measures rule-of-law stance, not an exposure.

evidence.quote: should not be bound by laws or court decisions that [he] thinks are wrong

claims.text: Military-intervention legitimacy item asks whether a hypothetical abusive incumbent entitles the armed forces to assume control; it registers a normative judgment conditioned on leader abuse, not a prediction of or exposure to a coup.

evidence.quote: take control of government when elected leaders abuse power

claims.text: Accountability-owner question for elected parliamentarians; the option list assigns ownership to executive, parliament/council, party, voters, or no one, so the observation contrasts who is normatively responsible for post-election performance rather than who in fact monitors.

evidence.quote: once elected, [members of Parliament] do their jobs?

claims.text: Parallel accountability-owner question for the president; the same owner categories but a different target allow comparing who is designated accountable for executive versus legislative performance without assuming the two share an answer domain.

Emergency-power justification item: acceptance of police/security enforcement of public health mandates is conditional on a declared health emergency and asks about temporary limitation of democratic freedoms, so agreement is not a general endorsement of policing.

evidence.quote: temporarily limit democracy or democratic freedoms

claims.text: Consent-to-recontact item records a stated willingness to be in follow-up surveys; it is a stated predisposition, with applicability restricted to respondents lacking a mobile number, and is not proof of future participation.

evidence.quote: Willing to participate in follow-up surveys

claims.text: The candor and threat items share interviewer-report grain but different referents (respondent's honesty vs interviewer's felt threat), so their joint use must not be read as a single interview-quality factor.

Both owner questions offer the executive as a possible owner of oversight for MPs, and the president as target; naming the executive for the legislature is structurally available, so divergent answers diagnose target-specific accountability reasoning rather than a single civic competence.

Both fields are conditional and scope-restricted: Q63B is inapplicable where the COVID module was not fielded, and Q97 is asked of every respondent; comparing them would conflate a routed COVID judgment with an always-asked sponsorship belief.

inquiries.question: Among interviews where the interviewer reports felt or physical threat, does the respondent's attributed sponsorship (state, party, or Afrobarometer/partner) co-vary with the threat report in a way that would distinguish a real pressure environment from a misattribution or random interviewer distress?
inquiries.alternatives: If threat reports concentrate where sponsorship is attributed to the state or a party, this supports an environment-of-pressure reading; if threat reports are flat across sponsor categories or concentrate among Afrobarometer-attributors, it supports interviewer-level or misattribution readings and defeats the pressure interpretation.
inquiries.ceiling: Interviewer-clustered data and country non-administration of Q63B-style routes are not qualified here; nothing on actual intimidation causation, and no numerics are asserted.
inquiries.route: S04 existing observation-scope and asked-eligible RAW owner; only after source route, design and roles qualified.

inquiries.question: Does anticipated harassment of a woman candidate select a different women's-rights priority and a different demand direction than a general-expansion stance, i.e., are hostile-environment perceivers more likely to name gender-based violence and demand more government action than those who expect little sanction?
inquiries.alternatives: If high anticipated sanction pairs with gender-based-violence priority and more-government demand, this supports a threat-to-priority linkage; if high-sanction respondents name structural issues (pay, property) or prefer the status quo, the sanction-expectation and policy-preference accounts are rival readings.
inquiries.ceiling: Cross-sectional metadata only; priority is capped-choice so nonselection does not imply low importance, and nothing establishes that expectations cause demand.
inquiries.route: S04 existing observation-scope and asked-eligible RAW owner; only after source route, design and roles qualified.

inquiries.question: Do respondents who assign legislative oversight to the executive also endorse presidential non-bindingness or conditional military takeover, indicating an executive-centered accountability frame, or do the two items dissociate?
inquiries.alternatives: A coherent executive-centered configuration (executive-owned oversight plus presidential latitude plus intervention legitimacy) supports a single frame; dissociation would show that owner designation about MPs is not a proxy for authoritarian legality and would defeat that transfer.
inquiries.ceiling: Owner categories are nominal with merged party/voter options; no causal inference and no claim that owner answers predict behavior.
inquiries.route: S04 existing observation-scope and asked-eligible RAW owner; only after source route, design and roles qualified.

existing_holds.why: Without these, the interviewer-grain encounter items cannot be read as environment indicators or as interviewer distress; the direction of any relation remains unidentified.

existing_holds.missing: Verified full-wave administration since the stems carry country-specific placeholders and Q28 carries a country non-asked code.
existing_holds.why: Cross-country comparability of the forced-choice legality and intervention items cannot be established from blended stem metadata alone.

existing_holds.missing: Confirmation of whether the two owner questions were co-administered in the same wave and country, since Q48A carries a country-date non-asked code.
existing_holds.why: A same-respondent comparison of presidential versus legislative oversight attribution presupposes joint administration that this metadata does not establish.

existing_holds.missing: The COV1 eligibility variable that routes Q63B to not applicable.

existing_holds.missing: Whether recontact willingness is conditioned on sponsor belief and on mobile availability across countries.
